Luke 1.summary: Luke addresses Theophilus and states that he has investigated traditions about Jesus to write an orderly account (Luke 1:1–4). During Herod's reign, Gabriel announces to the priest Zechariah that Elizabeth will bear John, who will prepare people for the Lord; Zechariah doubts and cannot speak (Luke 1:5–25). Gabriel then tells Mary that she will bear Jesus, the promised Davidic king, and Mary responds in trust (Luke 1:26–38). Mary visits Elizabeth, and her song praises God's mercy and reversal of human power (Luke 1:39–56). John is born and named; Zechariah's speech returns and he prophesies about God's deliverance and John's preparatory role (Luke 1:57–80). The opening places Jesus and John within Israel's hopes and depicts God working through people of modest standing.
Luke 1.whereWeAre: Mark's Gospel closed with the risen Jesus commissioning his followers and ascending to heaven, after which the women fled the tomb afraid (Mark 16:1-8,19-20). Luke opens his own orderly account differently, going back before Jesus' birth: the angel Gabriel announces John's birth to the priest Zechariah and then Mary's role as the mother of the promised Davidic king, and the chapter closes with John's birth and his father's prophecy (1:1-80). That birth of the forerunner sets up chapter 2's birth of the one he was sent to prepare for.

keyFigures.name: Zechariah
keyFigures.role: A priest who doubts Gabriel's announcement and is struck speechless, then regains his voice at John's birth to prophesy about God's promised deliverance (1:8-20,57-79).

keyFigures.name: Elizabeth
keyFigures.role: Conceives John in her old age, and when Mary visits her the baby leaps in her womb as she blesses Mary as the mother of her Lord (1:24-25,39-45).

keyFigures.name: Gabriel
keyFigures.role: An angel sent to announce John's birth to Zechariah and, six months later, Jesus' birth to Mary, naming Jesus the promised Son of the Highest (1:11-20,26-38).

keyFigures.name: Mary
keyFigures.role: A young virgin who accepts Gabriel's announcement in trust and sings a song praising God for lifting up the lowly and bringing down the proud (1:26-38,46-55).

keyFigures.name: John
keyFigures.role: Born to Zechariah and Elizabeth in their old age and named by his father's own written word, the child Zechariah's prophecy says will prepare the way of the Lord (1:57-66,76-79).

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Named by Gabriel before his birth as the promised Davidic king whose kingdom will never end (1:31-33).

keyThemes.explanation: Gabriel announces that Elizabeth's son John will prepare the way for the Lord, fulfilling Israel's long-held hope that God would act decisively through a chosen forerunner (1:5-17,67-79).

Zechariah doubts Gabriel's announcement and is struck silent, while Mary accepts an even more startling announcement with simple trust, pairing two very different responses to the same kind of impossible news (1:18-20,34-38).
Mary's song praises a God who scatters the proud, lifts up the lowly, and fills the hungry, framing Jesus' coming birth as part of a larger pattern of reversal (1:46-55).
John's birth restores Zechariah's speech, and his prophecy over the child links John's role as forerunner to God's larger promise of light and peace (1:57-66,76-80).

Luke 2.summary: Luke reports that an imperial registration brought Joseph and the pregnant Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, where Jesus was born and placed in a manger (Luke 2:1–7). Angels announce the birth to shepherds, who visit and spread the news (Luke 2:8–20). Jesus is circumcised and named on the eighth day, and later presented at the Jerusalem temple; Simeon and Anna praise God and speak about the child (Luke 2:21–40). When Jesus is twelve, he stays in the temple among teachers during Passover and speaks of his Father's affairs before returning with his parents (Luke 2:41–52). The chapter connects the infant and growing Jesus with Israel's worship and expectations.
Luke 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 ended with Zechariah's prophecy that his son John would prepare the way for God's promised deliverance (1:76-79). Chapter 2 delivers that deliverer: Jesus is born in Bethlehem during a Roman registration, shepherds and later Simeon and Anna recognize him, and at twelve he astonishes temple teachers with his understanding before returning home in obedience (2:1-52). Luke then jumps ahead about eighteen years to chapter 3, where John's own adult ministry finally begins.

keyFigures.name: Joseph
keyFigures.role: Travels with the pregnant Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem for the Roman registration and returns there each year for Passover (2:4-7,41-42).

keyFigures.name: Mary
keyFigures.role: Gives birth to Jesus in Bethlehem, treasures what she hears about him in her heart, and later searches anxiously for him when he stays behind in the temple (2:6-7,19,41-48).

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Born in Bethlehem and laid in a manger, then found at twelve astonishing the temple teachers with his understanding before returning home in obedience (2:7,46-51).

keyFigures.name: Shepherds
keyFigures.role: Hear an angel's announcement of Jesus' birth, visit the manger, and spread the news to everyone they meet (2:8-18).

keyFigures.name: Simeon
keyFigures.role: A devout man promised he would not die before seeing the Messiah, who takes the infant Jesus in his arms and praises God while warning Mary of coming sorrow (2:25-35).

keyFigures.name: Anna
keyFigures.role: An elderly prophetess who gives thanks for the infant Jesus and tells everyone waiting for Jerusalem's redemption about him (2:36-38).

keyThemes.explanation: Angels announce Jesus' birth first to shepherds, ordinary working people rather than rulers or priests, matching Luke's pattern of good news reaching the overlooked (2:8-20).
Joseph and Mary follow the law's requirements for circumcision and purification exactly, presenting Jesus at the temple like any other Jewish family would (2:21-24,39-42).
Simeon calls the infant Jesus a light to the Gentiles as well as the glory of Israel, extending Israel's hope beyond Israel itself from the very start (2:25-35).

At twelve, Jesus startles the temple teachers with his understanding and tells his worried parents he must be about his Father's business, foreshadowing his identity before his public ministry begins (2:46-52).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Both identify Bethlehem as the place of Jesus' birth.
Luke quotes the law consecrating every firstborn male to the Lord.

Luke 3.summary: Luke situates John's ministry among named Roman and local rulers, then depicts him preaching repentance and the forgiveness of sins in the Jordan region (Luke 3:1–6). John urges crowds to share, tax collectors to avoid overcharging, and soldiers to refuse extortion (Luke 3:7–14). He denies being the Messiah and announces one mightier than himself; Herod later imprisons him (Luke 3:15–20). Luke then describes Jesus' baptism, the descent of the Spirit, and a heavenly declaration (Luke 3:21–22), before giving a genealogy tracing Jesus' ancestry back to Adam (Luke 3:23–38). The chapter introduces Jesus' public role against a call for concrete moral change.
Luke 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 closed with the boy Jesus growing in wisdom and favor while John, though already born, was still years from his public ministry (2:52). Chapter 3 opens that ministry: John preaches repentance to crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers, denies being the Messiah, and is eventually imprisoned by Herod; Jesus is baptized, and Luke traces his ancestry all the way back to Adam (3:1-38). That baptism and genealogy, naming Jesus as God's Son and descendant of Adam, set up chapter 4's account of the devil's own direct challenge to that identity.

keyFigures.name: John the Baptist
keyFigures.role: Preaches repentance in the Jordan region, gives crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers practical instructions, and denies being the Messiah himself before Herod imprisons him (3:3-20).

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Is baptized, hears a heavenly voice name him God's beloved Son, and has his ancestry traced by Luke all the way back to Adam (3:21-38).

keyFigures.name: Herod Antipas
keyFigures.role: Rebuked by John for his marriage to Herodias, Herod responds by locking John up in prison (3:19-20).

keyFigures.name: Herodias
keyFigures.role: The woman whose marriage to Herod Antipas draws John's public rebuke (3:19).

keyFigures.name: Crowds, tax collectors and soldiers
keyFigures.role: Ask John what they should do, and he tells them to share what they have, overcharge no one, and be content with their wages (3:10-14).

keyFigures.name: Tiberius Caesar and Pilate
keyFigures.role: Named rulers Luke uses to date the start of John's ministry to around AD 28-29 (3:1-2).

keyThemes.explanation: John tells crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers that real repentance means sharing what they have and refusing to exploit others, not just feeling sorry (3:7-14).
John denies being the Christ himself and points instead to one far mightier who is coming, redirecting the crowd's hope away from himself (3:15-18).
As Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends and a voice from heaven names him God's beloved Son, publicly confirming his identity before his ministry begins (3:21-22).
Luke traces Jesus' ancestry all the way back to Adam, tying Jesus to the whole human family rather than stopping at Abraham as Matthew's genealogy does (3:23-38).

explainedReferences.explanation: Luke quotes Isaiah's voice in the wilderness preparing the Lord's way.
Luke quotes Isaiah's description of the prepared way and all flesh seeing God's salvation.
Same event: Jesus' baptism and the heavenly voice.

Luke 4.summary: Filled with the Spirit, Jesus faces the devil's temptations in the wilderness and responds with Scripture (Luke 4:1–13). He teaches in Galilee and reads Isaiah at Nazareth, announcing good news to the poor, release and the Lord's favor; the congregation first marvels and then grows hostile when he recalls God's mercy beyond Israel (Luke 4:14–30). At Capernaum Jesus teaches with authority, expels a demon, heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others, and insists on bringing the kingdom message to other towns (Luke 4:31–44). Luke portrays a Spirit-led mission defined by proclamation, healing, and controversy.
Luke 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 ended with a voice from heaven naming Jesus God's beloved Son, and a genealogy tracing him back to Adam (3:22,38). Chapter 4 tests that identity: the devil tempts Jesus in the wilderness, he reads Isaiah's words about good news for the poor in his hometown synagogue and is nearly thrown off a cliff for it, and in Capernaum he teaches with authority, heals, and casts out demons (4:1-44). That pattern of authority and controversy continues in chapter 5, where a miraculous catch of fish leads Simon, James, and John to leave everything and follow him.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Resists the devil's wilderness temptations with Scripture, reads Isaiah's promise of good news to the poor in the Nazareth synagogue, and teaches, heals, and casts out demons with authority in Capernaum (4:1-44).

keyFigures.name: The devil
keyFigures.role: Tempts Jesus three times in the wilderness, twisting Scripture in his final temptation, and departs only until a more opportune time (4:1-13).

keyFigures.name: Nazareth synagogue hearers
keyFigures.role: First marvel at Jesus' gracious words, then grow furious and try to throw him off a cliff when he recalls God's mercy reaching foreigners ahead of Israel (4:22-29).

keyFigures.name: Elijah and Elisha
keyFigures.role: Earlier prophets Jesus cites as having helped a foreign widow and healed a foreign leper rather than anyone in Israel, provoking his hometown's anger (4:25-27).

keyFigures.name: Simon
keyFigures.role: His mother-in-law is healed of a fever by Jesus in his own Capernaum home (4:38-39).

keyFigures.name: Demons
keyFigures.role: Recognize Jesus and are cast out of an afflicted man in the Capernaum synagogue and of many others brought to him at sunset (4:33-36,41).

keyThemes.explanation: The devil tempts Jesus three times in the wilderness, and each time Jesus answers with Scripture rather than his own reasoning (4:1-13).
Reading from Isaiah in the Nazareth synagogue, Jesus announces that the Scripture's promise of good news to the poor and freedom to the oppressed is fulfilled that very day, in him (4:16-21).
The same congregation that first marvels at Jesus turns furious when he reminds them that God once sent his prophets to help foreigners ahead of Israel's own people (4:22-30).
In Capernaum Jesus teaches with authority that amazes people, casts out an unclean spirit with a word, and heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others who are brought to him (4:31-44).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The temptation of Jesus in the wilderness, with different ordering.
Jesus quotes the teaching about not living by bread alone.
Jesus quotes the requirement to worship and serve the Lord alone.
The tempter quotes the psalm about angels providing protection.
Jesus quotes the command not to put the Lord to the test.
Jesus reads from Isaiah's passage concerning the anointed one bringing good news and liberation; the wording is not identical.
Jesus reads this passage in the synagogue at Nazareth.
Jesus reads Isaiah's proclamation of the acceptable year of the Lord; he does not quote the entire verse.

Luke 5.summary: Jesus directs Simon to a remarkable catch of fish and calls Simon, James and John to catch people; they leave their boats to follow him (Luke 5:1–11). Jesus cleanses a man with a serious skin condition and sends him to a priest, while crowds gather and Jesus withdraws to pray (Luke 5:12–16). He forgives and heals a paralyzed man amid objections from scribes and Pharisees (Luke 5:17–26). Jesus calls the tax collector Levi, eats with tax collectors and others, and answers questions about fasting with wedding and new-wine images (Luke 5:27–39). The chapter joins Jesus' call to discipleship with his authority to heal, forgive, and welcome outsiders.
Luke 5.whereWeAre: Chapter 4 ended with Jesus insisting he must preach the kingdom message in other towns too (4:43-44). Chapter 5 shows that mission drawing followers and critics alike: a miraculous catch of fish leads Simon, James, and John to leave their boats, Jesus heals and forgives a paralyzed man despite scribes' objections, and he calls the tax collector Levi while explaining his new teaching with images of wedding guests and new wine (5:1-39). Those objections sharpen in chapter 6, where Sabbath disputes lead Jesus to choose twelve apostles and deliver a sweeping sermon on the kingdom's values.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Calls fishermen to follow him after a miraculous catch, cleanses a man with a skin disease, forgives and heals a paralyzed man, and calls the tax collector Levi (5:1-32).

keyFigures.name: Simon Peter
keyFigures.role: Falls at Jesus' knees calling himself a sinful man after the miraculous catch of fish, then leaves his boats to follow him (5:8-11).

keyFigures.name: James and John
keyFigures.role: Simon's fishing partners who are equally astonished by the great catch and leave everything to follow Jesus alongside him (5:7-11).

keyFigures.name: Levi
keyFigures.role: A tax collector who leaves his booth the moment Jesus calls him and throws a great feast for him at his own house (5:27-29).

keyFigures.name: Paralyzed man and friends
keyFigures.role: His friends lower him through the roof tiles to reach Jesus, whose forgiveness and healing of the man prove his authority before watching scribes (5:18-25).

keyFigures.name: Scribes and Pharisees
keyFigures.role: Object that only God can forgive sins and criticize Jesus for eating with tax collectors and sinners (5:21,30).

keyThemes.explanation: A miraculous catch of fish convinces Simon, James, and John to leave their boats, and Levi leaves his tax booth just as quickly once Jesus calls him (5:1-11,27-28).
Jesus cleanses a man with a skin disease and forgives and heals a paralyzed man, pairing physical healing with the deeper claim that he has authority to forgive sins (5:12-26).
Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners and tells critics that he came to call sinners to repentance, not people who already consider themselves righteous (5:29-32).
Jesus compares his new teaching to new wine that cannot be poured into old wineskins, explaining why his disciples do not fast the way John's disciples or the Pharisees do (5:33-39).

Luke 6.summary: Disputes arise when Jesus' disciples pluck grain on the Sabbath and Jesus heals a man with a withered hand; Jesus speaks of his authority over the Sabbath and the value of doing good (Luke 6:1–11). After praying, he chooses twelve apostles (Luke 6:12–16). He addresses disciples and crowds with blessings for the poor and hungry, warnings to the rich and satisfied, love for enemies, mercy, nonjudgmental self-examination, good fruit, and obedience shown through action (Luke 6:17–49). The chapter presents an ethic of the kingdom that challenges ordinary ideas of status and retaliation.
Luke 6.whereWeAre: Chapter 5 ended with Jesus defending his disciples' new way of following him against the old patterns of fasting and patched garments (5:36-39). Chapter 6 shows that new way in full: Sabbath healings provoke his opponents, he chooses twelve apostles after a night of prayer, and he teaches a crowd blessings for the poor and hungry alongside warnings to the rich, love for enemies, and the need to act on what they hear (6:1-49). That sermon's call to build on a solid foundation leads into chapter 7's stories of people who respond to Jesus in faith.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Heals on the Sabbath, chooses twelve apostles after praying all night, and teaches a great sermon of blessings, warnings, and practical obedience (6:1-49).

keyFigures.name: The twelve apostles
keyFigures.role: Chosen by Jesus after a night of prayer to be his closest followers (6:12-16).

keyFigures.name: Scribes and Pharisees
keyFigures.role: Watch for grounds to accuse Jesus of breaking the Sabbath by picking grain and by healing a man's hand (6:1-2,6-7).

keyFigures.name: Man with a withered hand
keyFigures.role: Healed by Jesus in the synagogue despite his critics watching for a reason to accuse him (6:6-10).

keyFigures.name: Disciples and crowds
keyFigures.role: Hear Jesus' sermon of blessings for the poor and hungry, warnings to the rich, and the call to love enemies and build a life on his words (6:17-49).

keyThemes.explanation: When Pharisees object to the disciples picking grain and to a Sabbath healing, Jesus asks whether the Sabbath is for doing good or doing harm, not simply following rules (6:1-11).
Jesus blesses the poor, hungry, and weeping while warning the rich, full, and laughing, turning ordinary ideas of who is fortunate completely upside down (6:20-26).
Jesus tells his disciples to love their enemies, do good to those who hate them, and give without expecting anything back, matching the mercy of their own Father (6:27-36).
Jesus warns that calling him Lord means nothing without obeying him, comparing a life built on his words to a house built on solid rock (6:43-49).

explainedReferences.explanation: Jesus retells the incident of David eating the consecrated bread.

Luke 7.summary: Jesus heals a centurion's valued servant after Jewish elders and friends relay the officer's appeal; Jesus marvels at his faith (Luke 7:1–10). At Nain he raises a widow's only son, prompting awe and prophetic comparisons (Luke 7:11–17). John sends messengers asking whether Jesus is the expected one; Jesus points to works of restoration and praises John's prophetic role (Luke 7:18–35). At a Pharisee's meal, a woman known as a sinner washes Jesus' feet with tears and anoints them. Jesus tells a parable about forgiven debts and contrasts the woman's love with the host's limited hospitality (Luke 7:36–50). Faith, mercy, and varied responses to Jesus run through the chapter.
Luke 7.whereWeAre: Chapter 6 closed with Jesus warning that hearing his words without acting on them is like building a house with no foundation (6:46-49). Chapter 7 shows the foundation of faith in action: Jesus heals a centurion's servant because of the officer's trust, raises a widow's only son at Nain, answers John the Baptist's own doubts from prison, and lets a sinful woman's love at a Pharisee's table outshine his host's thin hospitality (7:1-50). That contrast between deep faith and shallow religion carries into chapter 8's parable of seed falling on different kinds of soil.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Heals a centurion's servant, raises a widow's son at Nain, answers John the Baptist's questions from prison, and forgives a sinful woman's many sins at a Pharisee's table (7:1-50).

keyFigures.name: Centurion
keyFigures.role: A Roman officer whose trust that Jesus can heal his servant with only a word leads Jesus to marvel at faith he has not found even in Israel (7:1-10).

keyFigures.name: Widow of Nain
keyFigures.role: Her only son is raised by Jesus from his own funeral procession, moving the crowd to praise God (7:11-17).

keyFigures.name: John the Baptist
keyFigures.role: Sends messengers from prison to ask whether Jesus is the promised one, and is praised by Jesus as more than a prophet once they leave (7:18-28).

keyFigures.name: Simon the Pharisee
keyFigures.role: Invites Jesus to dinner, privately doubts he is a prophet for letting a sinful woman touch him, and is told the parable of two forgiven debtors in response (7:36-43).

keyFigures.name: Woman known as a sinner
keyFigures.role: Weeps at Jesus' feet, washes them with her tears and hair, and is told her many sins are forgiven because she loved much (7:37-48).

keyThemes.explanation: A Roman centurion trusts that Jesus can heal his servant with only a word, and Jesus marvels that he has not found faith like this even in Israel (7:1-10).
Moved with compassion for a widow who has just lost her only son, Jesus raises the young man from his own funeral procession without even being asked (7:11-17).
When John's own disciples ask whether Jesus is the one who was promised, Jesus points to the healings and good news happening right in front of them as the answer (7:18-35).
A woman known as a sinner weeps at Jesus' feet and is forgiven much, and Jesus tells his host that the one who is forgiven much loves much in return (7:36-50).

explainedReferences.explanation: Jesus and Mark quote the prophecy about sending a messenger to prepare the way.

Luke 8.summary: Jesus travels preaching the kingdom accompanied by the Twelve and women who support the group, including Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Susanna (Luke 8:1–3). He teaches the sower parable and explains receptive hearing, then defines his family through those who hear and do God's word (Luke 8:4–21). He calms a storm on the lake (Luke 8:22–25), frees a man tormented by demons in the region of the Gerasenes (Luke 8:26–39), and heals a woman with prolonged bleeding while going to Jairus's house, where he raises Jairus's daughter (Luke 8:40–56). The chapter links hearing with faith and depicts authority over threatening forces.
Luke 8.whereWeAre: Chapter 7 ended with Jesus telling a forgiven woman that her faith had saved her, while his host Simon had offered little welcome at all (7:44-50). Chapter 8 widens that contrast: Jesus travels with the Twelve and the women who support his ministry, teaches that only some hearers let the word of God bear fruit, calms a storm, frees a man tormented by many demons, and heals a woman with bleeding on the way to raising Jairus's daughter (8:1-56). That combination of teaching and authority continues in chapter 9, where Jesus commissions the Twelve to do the same kind of work themselves.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Teaches the sower parable, calms a storm, frees a man tormented by demons, heals a bleeding woman, and raises Jairus's daughter (8:1-56).

keyFigures.name: The Twelve
keyFigures.role: Travel with Jesus and the women supporting his ministry, and are present through the storm, the Gerasene healing, and Jairus's house (8:1,22-25).

keyFigures.name: Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna
keyFigures.role: Women who travel with Jesus and support his ministry out of their own resources (8:1-3).

keyFigures.name: The possessed man
keyFigures.role: Freed by Jesus from many demons calling themselves Legion, then sent home to tell what God has done for him instead of staying with Jesus (8:26-39).

keyFigures.name: Jairus and his daughter
keyFigures.role: Jairus begs Jesus to heal his dying twelve-year-old daughter, and after she is reported dead Jesus takes her by the hand and raises her (8:41-42,49-56).

keyFigures.name: Woman with bleeding
keyFigures.role: Touches Jesus' garment after twelve years of illness, is healed instantly, and is called out publicly to confess what happened (8:43-48).

keyThemes.explanation: The parable of the sower pictures different hearers as different kinds of soil, warning that hearing God's word is not the same as letting it actually take root (8:4-18).
When told his mother and brothers are outside, Jesus says his true family is whoever hears God's word and does it, redefining kinship around obedience rather than blood (8:19-21).
Jesus calms a storm that terrifies the disciples and later tells a frightened Jairus not to fear but only to believe, pairing both moments as lessons in trusting him under pressure (8:22-25,40-56).
Once freed from the many demons controlling him, the man from the Gerasene region is sent home to tell everyone what God has done for him, becoming a witness instead of an outcast (8:26-39).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Jesus calming the storm on the lake.
Same event: Jesus raising Jairus' daughter and healing the woman with a flow of blood.
Same event: The woman healed of bleeding and Jairus's daughter raised.

Luke 9.summary: Jesus commissions the Twelve to proclaim God's kingdom and heal, and Herod wonders about Jesus' identity (Luke 9:1–9). Jesus feeds a large crowd, then receives Peter's confession that he is God's Messiah; he predicts suffering and calls followers to take up their cross (Luke 9:10–27). At the transfiguration Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus, and a voice tells the disciples to listen to him (Luke 9:28–36). Jesus heals a boy, predicts his betrayal, teaches greatness through welcoming a child, and corrects exclusionary attitudes (Luke 9:37–50). As he sets his face toward Jerusalem, he refuses retaliatory violence and emphasizes the cost of following (Luke 9:51–62).
Luke 9.whereWeAre: Chapter 8 ended with Jesus raising Jairus's daughter and ordering her parents to tell no one (8:54-56). Chapter 9 sends that same authority outward: Jesus commissions the Twelve to preach and heal, feeds a crowd of five thousand, receives Peter's confession that he is God's Messiah, is transfigured before three disciples, and begins setting his face toward Jerusalem despite a Samaritan village's refusal to welcome him (9:1-62). That turn toward Jerusalem opens the travel narrative chapter 10 continues with the sending of seventy more messengers.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Commissions the Twelve, feeds five thousand, is transfigured, heals a boy the disciples could not help, and sets his face toward Jerusalem (9:1-62).

keyFigures.name: The Twelve
keyFigures.role: Are sent out to preach and heal, witness the feeding of five thousand, and argue among themselves about who is greatest (9:1-17,46).

keyFigures.name: Peter
keyFigures.role: Confesses that Jesus is God's Messiah and witnesses the transfiguration alongside James and John (9:20,28-33).

keyFigures.name: Moses and Elijah
keyFigures.role: Appear with Jesus at the transfiguration, speaking with him about his coming death in Jerusalem (9:30-31).

keyFigures.name: James and John
keyFigures.role: Witness the transfiguration with Peter and later ask Jesus to call down fire on a Samaritan village that refused to welcome him (9:28,54).

keyFigures.name: Boy and father
keyFigures.role: The father begs Jesus to heal his son after the disciples could not, and Jesus casts out the spirit and gives the boy back to him (9:38-42).

keyThemes.explanation: Jesus sends the Twelve out to preach and heal while taking nothing for the journey, teaching them to depend on the hospitality of those they serve (9:1-6).
Peter rightly calls Jesus God's Messiah, but Jesus immediately redefines that title around coming suffering, death, and a cross every follower must also carry (9:18-27).
At the transfiguration, a voice from the cloud names Jesus God's Son and commands the disciples simply to listen to him, even with Moses and Elijah standing right beside him (9:28-36).
The disciples argue about who is greatest and want to call down fire on an unwelcoming village, and Jesus answers both with lessons in humility rather than rivalry or retaliation (9:46-56).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Jesus feeding about five thousand with five loaves and two fish.
Same event: The feeding of the five thousand.
Same event: Peter's confession of Jesus' identity.
Same event: The transfiguration and the appearance of Moses and Elijah.

Luke 10.summary: Jesus appoints seventy or seventy-two others (depending on manuscript tradition) and sends them ahead in pairs, warning of rejection and instructing them to announce God's kingdom (Luke 10:1–24). A legal expert asks about eternal life, and Jesus uses the story of a compassionate Samaritan to define neighborly action, even across hostile boundaries (Luke 10:25–37). At the home of Martha, Mary listens at Jesus' feet while Martha is distracted by serving; Jesus says Mary has chosen the better portion (Luke 10:38–42). Mission, mercy, and attentive listening characterize the chapter.
Luke 10.whereWeAre: Chapter 9 closed with Jesus warning that no one who looks back after starting the journey is fit for God's kingdom (9:61-62). Chapter 10 continues that same journey: Jesus sends out seventy or seventy-two messengers ahead of him, a legal expert's question about the law leads to the parable of the compassionate Samaritan, and at Martha and Mary's home Jesus commends Mary for choosing to listen rather than stay busy serving (10:1-42). That praise for attentive listening leads directly into chapter 11's request from a disciple to be taught how to pray.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Sends out seventy or seventy-two messengers, answers a legal expert's question with the parable of the compassionate Samaritan, and commends Mary for listening at his feet (10:1-42).

keyFigures.name: Seventy or seventy-two disciples
keyFigures.role: Sent out ahead of Jesus in pairs and return rejoicing that even demons obeyed them in his name (10:1,17).

keyFigures.name: Legal expert
keyFigures.role: Asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life and then, trying to justify himself, asks who counts as his neighbor (10:25-29).

keyFigures.name: Samaritan
keyFigures.role: A fictional traveler in Jesus' parable who stops to help a wounded stranger when a priest and a Levite both pass by, becoming the story's example of a true neighbor (10:30-37).

keyFigures.name: Martha
keyFigures.role: Welcomes Jesus into her home and complains that her sister has left her to do all the serving alone (10:38-40).

keyFigures.name: Mary
keyFigures.role: Sits at Jesus' feet listening instead of helping her sister Martha serve, and is told she has chosen the better part (10:39,42).

keyThemes.explanation: Jesus sends seventy or seventy-two messengers ahead of him in pairs, warning them of rejection but relying on whatever household welcomes them to receive their message (10:1-12).
When the seventy return thrilled that demons obeyed them, Jesus redirects their joy toward the far greater fact that their names are written in heaven (10:17-24).
Asked who counts as a neighbor, Jesus answers with a despised Samaritan who stops to help a wounded stranger when a priest and a Levite both pass by (10:25-37).
Martha is busy serving while Mary sits listening at Jesus' feet, and Jesus says Mary has chosen the one thing that is truly needed (10:38-42).

explainedReferences.explanation: The lawyer quotes the command to love God with heart, soul, strength and mind.
The command to love one's neighbor as oneself is directly quoted.

Luke 11.summary: Jesus teaches a prayer centered on God's name, kingdom, daily provision, forgiveness, and deliverance; he illustrates persistence in asking and God's willingness to give good gifts (Luke 11:1–13). After an exorcism, opponents accuse him of acting by Beelzebul, and Jesus answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand and calls hearers to respond rightly to his message (Luke 11:14–32). He speaks about a healthy eye and inner light (Luke 11:33–36). At a Pharisee's meal, he denounces outward religious display that neglects justice and love, and rebukes legal experts for burdens and obstacles they place on others (Luke 11:37–54).
Luke 11.whereWeAre: Chapter 10 ended with Jesus telling Martha that Mary had chosen the better part by sitting and listening to him (10:38-42). Chapter 11 opens with a disciple asking to be taught to pray the same way Mary listened, and Jesus gives them the Lord's Prayer before an exorcism draws the charge that he acts by Beelzebul; at a Pharisee's meal he denounces outward religious display that neglects justice and love (11:1-54). That public confrontation sets up chapter 12's private warning to the disciples about the same group's hypocrisy.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Teaches the Lord's Prayer, answers an accusation that he casts out demons by Beelzebul, and denounces Pharisees and legal experts for neglecting justice while loading others with burdens (11:1-54).

keyFigures.name: Disciples
keyFigures.role: Ask Jesus to teach them to pray as John taught his own disciples (11:1).

keyFigures.name: Accusers in the crowd
keyFigures.role: Claim Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebul, prompting his answer that a divided kingdom cannot stand (11:15).

keyFigures.name: Pharisee host
keyFigures.role: Invites Jesus to a meal and is surprised that he does not wash before eating, drawing Jesus' rebuke of outward religious display (11:37-39).

keyFigures.name: Pharisees and legal experts
keyFigures.role: Receive Jesus' series of woes for tithing herbs while neglecting justice, and for locking away the key of knowledge (11:42-52).

keyFigures.name: Jonah and queen of the South
keyFigures.role: Figures from Israel's own Scriptures Jesus cites as examples who responded to far less revelation than the crowd before him now has (11:29-32).

keyThemes.explanation: Jesus teaches the Lord's Prayer and promises that God gives good gifts, especially the Holy Spirit, to those who keep asking (11:1-13).

Accused of casting out demons by Beelzebul, Jesus answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand and warns that people who see God's work and still demand another sign have already missed the point (11:14-32).
Jesus condemns Pharisees for cleaning the outside of the cup while their hearts stay full of greed, insisting that inner integrity matters more than outward display (11:33-44).
Jesus rebukes legal experts for loading people with burdens they themselves will not lift a finger to carry, and for locking away the very knowledge they were meant to share (11:45-54).

Luke 12.summary: Jesus warns disciples about hypocrisy, urges fearless witness, and assures them of God's care (Luke 12:1–12). A dispute over inheritance prompts the rich fool parable, challenging wealth accumulation without regard for God (Luke 12:13–21). Jesus teaches against anxiety, encourages generosity and heavenly treasure, and calls followers to readiness like alert servants awaiting their master (Luke 12:22–48). He speaks of the division his mission will bring and urges discernment of the times and reconciliation (Luke 12:49–59). The chapter tests what people trust and whether that trust shapes how they live.
Luke 12.whereWeAre: Chapter 11 ended with Pharisees and legal experts watching Jesus closely, hoping to trap him in something he said (11:53-54). Chapter 12 shows Jesus turning to warn his own disciples first: he tells them not to fear those who can only kill the body, refuses to settle an inheritance dispute and instead tells the parable of the rich fool, and calls them to trust God's care over anxiety while staying ready for his return (12:1-59). That same urgency about readiness carries into chapter 13's call to repent before it is too late.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Warns his disciples against hypocrisy, tells the parable of the rich fool, teaches trust over anxiety, and calls for readiness like servants awaiting their master (12:1-59).

keyFigures.name: Disciples
keyFigures.role: Are warned not to fear those who can only kill the body and are assured that God cares for them more than for sparrows (12:4-7).

keyFigures.name: Man requesting inheritance division
keyFigures.role: Asks Jesus to make his brother divide their inheritance, prompting the parable of the rich fool instead (12:13-14).

keyFigures.name: Rich fool
keyFigures.role: A fictional farmer in Jesus' parable who plans bigger barns the same night his life is required of him, illustrating the danger of storing up wealth without regard for God (12:16-21).

keyFigures.name: Servants and master
keyFigures.role: Fictional figures in Jesus' parables about readiness, where faithful servants are rewarded and one entrusted with much is held to a stricter account (12:35-48).

keyFigures.name: Crowds
keyFigures.role: Hear Jesus call them to discern the present time the way they already read the weather, and to settle disputes before they escalate (12:54-59).

keyThemes.explanation: Jesus warns his disciples against the hidden hypocrisy of the Pharisees, promising that everything covered up will eventually be made known (12:1-12).

Asked to settle an inheritance dispute, Jesus instead tells of a rich man who plans bigger barns the same night his life is required of him, warning that life does not consist of possessions (12:13-21).
Jesus tells his disciples not to worry about food or clothing, since the God who feeds ravens and clothes lilies can be trusted to provide for them too (12:22-34).
Jesus compares faithful disciples to servants who keep watch for their master's return, warning that the one entrusted with more will be held to a stricter account (12:35-48).

Luke 13.summary: Jesus rejects the assumption that victims of Pilate's violence or a falling tower were worse sinners than others and calls everyone to repent (Luke 13:1–5). A barren fig tree parable warns that time for change should not be presumed unlimited (Luke 13:6–9). He heals a bent woman on the Sabbath despite a synagogue leader's objection, then compares the kingdom to mustard seed and leaven (Luke 13:10–21). On the journey to Jerusalem, Jesus urges entering through the narrow door and laments Jerusalem's resistance to prophetic appeals (Luke 13:22–35).
Luke 13.whereWeAre: Chapter 12 ended with Jesus urging his hearers to settle matters quickly, before it is too late to be reconciled (12:57-59). Chapter 13 presses that urgency further: Jesus rejects the idea that victims of a recent tragedy were worse sinners than anyone else and calls everyone to repent, heals a bent woman on the Sabbath over a synagogue leader's objection, and as he journeys on grieves over Jerusalem's history of rejecting the prophets sent to it (13:1-35). That lament continues in chapter 14, set at the table of one more Pharisee who watches Jesus closely.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Calls everyone to repent rather than judge recent tragedy victims as worse sinners, heals a bent woman on the Sabbath, and laments over Jerusalem on his way there (13:1-35).

keyFigures.name: Galileans killed by Pilate and Siloam victims
keyFigures.role: Recent tragedy victims people cite to Jesus, who turns their deaths into a call for everyone's own repentance rather than a judgment on the victims (13:1-5).

keyFigures.name: Woman bent for eighteen years
keyFigures.role: Healed by Jesus on the Sabbath and immediately stands up straight to praise God (13:11-13).

keyFigures.name: Synagogue leader
keyFigures.role: Objects to Jesus healing on the Sabbath, only to be answered that even animals are untied and watered on that day (13:14-16).

keyFigures.name: Herod
keyFigures.role: Reported to want Jesus dead, prompting Jesus to call him "that fox" and insist he will finish his work regardless (13:31-32).

keyFigures.name: Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: The city Jesus addresses directly in his closing lament over its history of killing the prophets sent to it (13:34-35).

keyThemes.theme: Suffering is not a simple moral score
keyThemes.explanation: Jesus rejects the idea that people killed by Pilate or by a falling tower were worse sinners than anyone else, turning the question back into a call for everyone to repent (13:1-5).
The parable of the barren fig tree warns that patience for change has a limit, even when a gardener pleads for one more year (13:6-9).
Jesus heals a woman bent over for eighteen years on the Sabbath and asks whether this daughter of Abraham deserves less consideration than an ox led to water (13:10-17).
The mustard seed and leaven picture a kingdom that starts small, while Jesus warns that many who expect to enter it by birthright will instead find the door shut (13:18-30).

Luke 14.summary: At a Sabbath meal in a Pharisee leader's home, Jesus heals a man with swelling and challenges objections to healing (Luke 14:1–6). Noticing guests seek honored seats, he teaches humility and asks hosts to invite people who cannot repay them (Luke 14:7–14). He tells the great banquet parable, in which invited guests make excuses and others are welcomed (Luke 14:15–24). Turning to crowds, he warns that following him requires decisive allegiance, self-denial, and counting the cost, illustrated by a builder and a king assessing their resources (Luke 14:25–35).
Luke 14.whereWeAre: Chapter 13 ended with Jesus grieving that Jerusalem was not willing to be gathered the way a hen gathers her chicks (13:34-35). Chapter 14 shows that resistance playing out at a Pharisee leader's Sabbath table: Jesus heals a man despite the objection, teaches humility about seating and hospitality toward people who cannot repay it, tells of a great banquet whose invited guests make excuses, and warns crowds to count the cost of following him (14:1-35). That demand for total commitment sets up chapter 15's parables defending why Jesus welcomes people who seem to have little to offer him.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Heals a man with dropsy at a Sabbath meal, teaches humility and hospitality toward people who cannot repay it, and warns crowds to count the cost of following him (14:1-35).

keyFigures.name: Pharisee leader
keyFigures.role: Hosts the Sabbath meal where Jesus heals and teaches, watching him closely throughout (14:1).

keyFigures.name: Man with dropsy (swelling)
keyFigures.role: Healed by Jesus at the Pharisee leader's table despite the Sabbath (14:2-4).

keyFigures.name: Guests and host
keyFigures.role: Hear Jesus teach that grabbing the seat of honor risks public humiliation, while inviting people who cannot repay brings a different kind of reward (14:7-14).

keyFigures.name: Invited guests and host in the banquet
keyFigures.role: Fictional figures in Jesus' parable of the great supper, where the first invited guests make excuses and the host fills his table with the poor and overlooked instead (14:16-24).

keyFigures.name: Crowds
keyFigures.role: Warned by Jesus that following him requires carrying a cross and counting the cost the way a builder or a king would before committing (14:25-33).

keyThemes.explanation: Jesus heals a man with dropsy on the Sabbath and asks the watching lawyers and Pharisees whether mercy can ever really wait for a more convenient day (14:1-6).
Watching guests grab the places of honor, Jesus teaches that whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (14:7-11).

Jesus tells his host to invite the poor and disabled instead of people who can repay the invitation, then pictures a great banquet filled with exactly those kinds of guests after the invited ones make excuses (14:12-24).
Jesus warns large crowds that following him means carrying a cross, and compares the decision to a builder or a king who first counts whether they have enough to finish what they start (14:25-35).

Luke 15.summary: Religious critics complain that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them (Luke 15:1–2). He answers with three stories: a shepherd searches for one lost sheep, a woman searches for one lost coin, and a father welcomes a lost son while an older son resents the celebration (Luke 15:3–32). Each story turns on loss, recovery, and joy, while the final parable exposes bitterness toward mercy. The chapter urges readers to consider both those needing restoration and those unwilling to rejoice when others return.
Luke 15.whereWeAre: Chapter 14 ended with Jesus warning that whoever does not renounce all he has cannot be his disciple (14:33-35). Chapter 15 answers why Jesus associates with people who seem to have renounced nothing at all: when Pharisees and scribes complain that he welcomes sinners, he tells three stories of a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son, each ending in celebration over what was found, while the last parable's resentful older brother leaves the question of joining unanswered (15:1-32). That same tension between joy and resentment continues into chapter 16's warnings about wealth.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Tells three parables of a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son to answer why he welcomes sinners and eats with them (15:1-32).

keyFigures.name: Tax collectors and sinners
keyFigures.role: Draw near to hear Jesus, prompting the religious leaders' complaint that leads to his three parables (15:1).

keyFigures.name: Pharisees and scribes
keyFigures.role: Complain that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them, the criticism his three parables directly answer (15:2).

keyFigures.name: Shepherd and woman
keyFigures.role: Fictional searchers in Jesus' parables who leave everything to find one lost sheep or one lost coin and then celebrate with their neighbors (15:4-9).

keyFigures.name: Father, younger son, older son
keyFigures.role: A fictional family in which a father runs to welcome home a son who wasted his inheritance, while the older son refuses to join the celebration (15:11-32).

keyThemes.explanation: A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to search for one lost sheep, and a woman sweeps her whole house for one lost coin, both searching as if the one missing piece mattered most (15:3-10).
Jesus says heaven rejoices more over one repentant sinner than over many who never felt they needed to return, the same point both the lost sheep and lost coin make (15:7-10).
A father runs to meet his returning son before the son can even finish his rehearsed apology, celebrating a reunion the son himself assumed was impossible (15:11-24).
The older brother refuses to join the celebration for his returned brother, and the parable ends without saying whether he ever goes in, leaving the question open for Jesus' own critics (15:25-32).

Luke 16.summary: Jesus tells the parable of a manager facing dismissal who reduces debts to secure future hospitality; he uses it to teach shrewdness and faithfulness in handling money, not to endorse dishonesty (Luke 16:1–13). Addressing money-loving Pharisees, he says people cannot serve both God and wealth and speaks about the Law, the kingdom, and divorce (Luke 16:14–18). He then contrasts a rich man living in luxury with Lazarus, a suffering poor man at his gate; after death their situations are reversed, and Abraham insists that Moses and the prophets provide sufficient warning (Luke 16:19–31).
Luke 16.whereWeAre: Chapter 15 ended with a father pleading for his resentful older son to join the celebration over a brother who was dead and is alive again (15:25-32). Chapter 16 turns to money: Jesus tells of a dismissed manager who secures his future by reducing others' debts, warns money-loving Pharisees that no one can serve both God and wealth, and contrasts a rich man's comfortable life with the poor man Lazarus at his gate, whose situations are completely reversed after death (16:1-31). That reversal leads into chapter 17's teaching on a kingdom that arrives differently than expected.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Tells the parable of the shrewd manager, warns that no one can serve both God and wealth, and tells of the rich man and Lazarus (16:1-31).

keyFigures.name: Manager and rich employer
keyFigures.role: Fictional figures in Jesus' parable in which a manager facing dismissal reduces others' debts to secure his own future (16:1-8).

keyFigures.name: Pharisees
keyFigures.role: Ridicule Jesus' teaching about money because they love it themselves, drawing his warning that what people value highly can be detestable to God (16:14-15).

keyFigures.name: Rich man and Lazarus
keyFigures.role: Figures in Jesus' account of a rich man who ignores the suffering beggar at his own gate, only to have their situations completely reversed after death (16:19-23).

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Speaks to the rich man in the afterlife, explaining that a great gulf now separates them and that his brothers already have Moses and the prophets to warn them (16:24-31).

keyThemes.explanation: A dismissed manager secures his own future by reducing what others owe his master, and Jesus uses his shrewdness, not his dishonesty, as the lesson for handling money wisely (16:1-13).
Jesus tells money-loving Pharisees that no one can serve both God and wealth, since loyalty to one will eventually crowd out the other (16:10-15).
A rich man feasts every day while the poor man Lazarus lies at his very gate, and after death their situations are completely and permanently reversed (16:19-26).
Abraham tells the rich man that if his brothers will not listen to Moses and the prophets, nothing, not even someone rising from the dead, will persuade them either (16:27-31).

Luke 17.summary: Jesus warns against causing others to stumble and commands repeated forgiveness of a repentant person (Luke 17:1–4). He speaks about faith like a mustard seed and a servant's unpretentious duty (Luke 17:5–10). Traveling near Samaria and Galilee, Jesus cleanses ten people with skin disease; only one, identified as a Samaritan, returns to thank him (Luke 17:11–19). When questioned about the kingdom's arrival, Jesus describes its presence and warns disciples not to chase sensational claims, using images of sudden judgment from Noah and Lot (Luke 17:20–37).
Luke 17.whereWeAre: Chapter 16 ended with Abraham telling the rich man that if his brothers will not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither would someone risen from the dead persuade them (16:27-31). Chapter 17 shows persuasion already failing in small ways: Jesus warns against causing others to stumble, heals ten people with a skin disease but sees only one, a Samaritan, return to give thanks, and warns that the kingdom's and the Son of man's coming will be sudden, not something to chase after on rumor (17:1-37). That warning continues in chapter 18's call to persistent, humble prayer in the meantime.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Warns against causing others to stumble, heals ten people with a skin disease, and teaches that the kingdom's arrival and his own coming will be sudden (17:1-37).

keyFigures.name: Apostles
keyFigures.role: Ask Jesus to increase their faith, and are told that faith as small as a mustard seed is already enough (17:5-6).

keyFigures.name: Ten people with skin disease
keyFigures.role: Call out to Jesus for mercy and are healed as they go to show themselves to the priests (17:12-14).

keyFigures.name: Samaritan man
keyFigures.role: The only one of the ten healed who returns to thank Jesus, making the outsider the story's one example of gratitude (17:15-16).

keyFigures.name: Pharisees
keyFigures.role: Ask Jesus when the kingdom of God will come, and are told it is already in their midst rather than a spectacle to watch for (17:20-21).

keyFigures.name: Noah and Lot
keyFigures.role: Figures from Israel's own history Jesus cites as examples of sudden judgment arriving while ordinary life went on unaware (17:26-30).

keyThemes.explanation: Jesus warns against causing others to stumble and commands forgiving a repentant person again and again, even seven times in one day (17:1-4).
Jesus says a servant who only does his duty deserves no special thanks, teaching that even great faith is simply what disciples owe, not a reason for pride (17:5-10).
Of ten people healed of a skin disease, only the Samaritan comes back to thank Jesus, making the outsider the one example of real gratitude in the story (17:11-19).
Jesus says the kingdom of God is already in their midst, not a spectacle to go chasing after, and warns that his own coming will be as sudden and inescapable as the flood in Noah's day (17:20-37).

Luke 18.summary: Jesus tells a story about a widow seeking justice from an unjust judge to teach persistence in prayer (Luke 18:1–8). He contrasts a self-confident Pharisee's prayer with a tax collector's plea for mercy, then welcomes children whom disciples would turn away (Luke 18:9–17). A wealthy ruler asks about eternal life but grieves when told to sell his possessions and follow; Jesus discusses the difficulty of wealth and the reward of discipleship (Luke 18:18–30). He predicts his suffering and resurrection, though the disciples do not understand, and restores the sight of a blind beggar near Jericho (Luke 18:31–43).
Luke 18.whereWeAre: Chapter 17 ended with Jesus warning that on the day of the Son of man's coming, people must not look back, remembering Lot's wife (17:28-37). Chapter 18 teaches how to wait for that day rightly: a persistent widow's story teaches prayer that does not give up, a humble tax collector's prayer is accepted over a self-confident Pharisee's, Jesus welcomes children and tells a wealthy ruler to sell his possessions, and nearing Jericho he restores a blind beggar's sight (18:1-43). That healed beggar leads into chapter 19's account of another outcast near Jericho, the tax collector Zacchaeus.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Tells parables on persistent prayer and humble prayer, welcomes children, calls a wealthy ruler to sell his possessions, and heals a blind beggar near Jericho (18:1-43).

keyFigures.name: Widow and unjust judge
keyFigures.role: Fictional figures in Jesus' parable in which a persistent widow wears down an unjust judge simply by refusing to give up (18:2-5).

keyFigures.name: Pharisee and tax collector
keyFigures.role: Fictional worshippers in Jesus' comparison, where the Pharisee prays about his own righteousness and the tax collector simply begs for mercy (18:10-13).

keyFigures.name: Children and caregivers
keyFigures.role: Brought to Jesus for a blessing, and he rebukes the disciples who try to turn them away (18:15-16).

keyFigures.name: Wealthy ruler
keyFigures.role: Asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life, then goes away sad rather than sell his great possessions (18:18,23).

keyFigures.name: Blind beggar near Jericho
keyFigures.role: Calls out to Jesus despite the crowd's rebuke and receives his sight for his faith (18:35-43).

keyThemes.explanation: A persistent widow wears down an unjust judge simply by refusing to stop asking, and Jesus says God will surely answer his own people who cry out day and night (18:1-8).
A Pharisee thanks God for his own righteousness while a tax collector simply begs for mercy, and Jesus says the tax collector, not the Pharisee, goes home right with God (18:9-14).
Jesus welcomes children the disciples try to turn away, saying God's kingdom belongs to whoever receives it as simply as a child does (18:15-17).
A wealthy ruler goes away sad rather than sell his possessions, and Jesus says what is impossible for people to do on their own, God can still accomplish (18:18-30).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The encounter with a wealthy ruler.
Jesus repeats the command to honor father and mother.
The command against murder is explicitly repeated.
The command against adultery is explicitly repeated.
The command against stealing is explicitly repeated.
The command against false witness is explicitly repeated.
Same event: Jesus healing a blind man near Jericho, but chronology/location differs slightly.

Luke 19.summary: At Jericho, Jesus calls the tax collector Zacchaeus down from a tree and accepts hospitality at his home. Zacchaeus declares restitution and generosity; Jesus speaks of salvation reaching the household (Luke 19:1–10). Near Jerusalem Jesus tells the parable of a nobleman entrusting money to servants before receiving kingship, warning about accountability while also depicting violent royal power (Luke 19:11–27). Jesus enters Jerusalem amid praise, weeps over its coming devastation, and drives sellers from the temple, where he teaches despite opposition (Luke 19:28–48).
Luke 19.whereWeAre: Chapter 18 ended with a blind beggar near Jericho receiving his sight and the crowd giving praise to God (18:35-43). Chapter 19 finds another outcast in that same city: Jesus calls Zacchaeus the tax collector down from a tree and brings salvation to his house, tells a parable about servants held accountable for what they were given, and enters Jerusalem amid praise before weeping over the city and driving sellers from the temple (19:1-48). That temple confrontation sets up chapter 20's direct challenges from the leaders who run it.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Calls Zacchaeus down from a tree, tells the parable of the nobleman's entrusted money, enters Jerusalem weeping over it, and drives sellers from the temple (19:1-48).

keyFigures.name: Zacchaeus
keyFigures.role: A chief tax collector who climbs a tree to see Jesus, welcomes him joyfully, and pledges to repay everyone he has cheated four times over (19:2-8).

keyFigures.name: Crowd and disciples
keyFigures.role: Grumble that Jesus is staying with a sinner in Zacchaeus's house, then spread cloaks on the road and praise God as Jesus enters Jerusalem (19:7,36-37).

keyFigures.name: Nobleman, servants and citizens
keyFigures.role: Fictional figures in Jesus' parable about a nobleman who rewards servants who invested what he gave them and judges the citizens who rejected his rule (19:12-27).

keyFigures.name: Temple merchants
keyFigures.role: Buyers and sellers driven out of the temple courts by Jesus, who insists the temple was meant to be a house of prayer (19:45-46).

keyFigures.name: Religious leaders
keyFigures.role: Look for a way to destroy Jesus but cannot find one, since the people hang on his every word in the temple (19:47-48).

keyThemes.explanation: Zacchaeus climbs a tree just to see Jesus and ends up pledging to repay everyone he has cheated four times over, prompting Jesus to say that salvation has come to his house (19:1-10).
A nobleman's servants are rewarded or rebuked based on what they did with the money entrusted to them while he was away, a picture of accountability for the time before Jesus returns (19:11-27).
As Jesus approaches Jerusalem he weeps over it, warning that the city failed to recognize the things that would have brought it peace (19:28-44).
Jesus drives sellers from the temple, insisting it was meant to be a house of prayer rather than a marketplace, and then teaches there despite the leaders' anger (19:45-48).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The entry into Jerusalem and the people's praise.
The declaration blessing the one who comes in the Lord's name is repeated.
Jesus quotes God's designation of his house as a house of prayer.
Jesus quotes Jeremiah's phrase describing the temple as a den of thieves.

Luke 20.summary: Religious authorities challenge Jesus' right to teach in the temple; he asks about John's baptism, and they decline to answer (Luke 20:1–8). He tells the tenants parable, in which renters abuse messengers and kill the owner's son, drawing opposition from leaders (Luke 20:9–19). Jesus answers a trap about Roman taxes by distinguishing Caesar's claims from God's, then disputes with Sadducees over resurrection and marriage (Luke 20:20–40). He asks how the Messiah is David's son and Lord, and warns against scribes who seek honor while exploiting widows (Luke 20:41–47).
Luke 20.whereWeAre: Chapter 19 ended with religious leaders looking for a way to destroy Jesus because the people hung on his every word in the temple (19:47-48). Chapter 20 shows that opposition taking shape in public debate: leaders challenge his authority, his parable of the tenant farmers who kill the owner's son exposes them further, and he answers trap questions about Roman taxes and resurrection before warning against scribes who exploit widows while seeking honor (20:1-47). That warning leads directly into chapter 21's praise for a poor widow who gives everything she has.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Is challenged over his authority, tells the parable of the wicked tenants, answers trap questions about taxes and resurrection, and warns against scribes who exploit widows (20:1-47).

keyFigures.name: Chief priests, scribes and elders
keyFigures.role: Challenge Jesus' authority in the temple, recognize themselves in his parable of the wicked tenants, and are warned by him for exploiting widows while seeking honor (20:1-19,45-47).

keyFigures.name: Tenant farmers, owner and son
keyFigures.role: Fictional figures in Jesus' parable in which renters beat the owner's servants and kill his son, a story the leaders recognize is told against them (20:9-16).

keyFigures.name: Spies
keyFigures.role: Sent to trap Jesus into saying something treasonous about paying tribute to Caesar (20:20-22).

keyFigures.name: Sadducees
keyFigures.role: Challenge belief in the resurrection with a hypothetical widow married to seven brothers, and are told they misunderstand both Scripture and God's power (20:27-38).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: The scriptural king Jesus cites as calling the Messiah his Lord, questioning the assumption that the Messiah is merely David's son (20:41-44).

keyThemes.explanation: When leaders demand to know Jesus' authority, his parable of tenants who kill the owner's son answers by exposing exactly what they themselves are doing to him (20:1-19).
Asked whether paying tax to Caesar is lawful, Jesus says to give Caesar what is Caesar's and God what is God's, refusing to let the question trap him into taking only one side (20:20-26).
Sadducees try to make resurrection sound absurd with a hypothetical widow, but Jesus answers that God is not a God of the dead but of the living, since all live to him (20:27-40).
Jesus warns against scribes who make a show of long prayers while exploiting widows, pairing their outward religion with real harm done to the vulnerable (20:45-47).

explainedReferences.explanation: The rejected stone becoming the cornerstone is directly quoted.
The questioners explicitly cite Moses' rule requiring a brother to marry his deceased brother's widow.
Jesus references the burning-bush declaration naming the patriarchs.
Same event: These passages explicitly quote David's statement about sitting at the Lord's right hand.

Luke 21.summary: Jesus notices a poor widow offering two small coins and contrasts her gift with larger contributions of wealthier people (Luke 21:1–4). As others admire the temple, he predicts its destruction and warns of upheaval, persecution, and misleading claims (Luke 21:5–19). He speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, distress, and the times of the Gentiles, then uses cosmic imagery and the fig tree to urge vigilance and hope (Luke 21:20–36). Luke closes by noting Jesus' daily teaching at the temple and nights on the Mount of Olives (Luke 21:37–38).
Luke 21.whereWeAre: Chapter 20 ended with Jesus warning that scribes who devour widows' houses while making long prayers will receive greater condemnation (20:45-47). Chapter 21 immediately sets a poor widow's own small gift against that warning: Jesus praises her two coins as greater than the wealthy's large contributions, then predicts the temple's destruction and describes wars, persecution, and cosmic upheaval before urging watchfulness rather than despair (21:1-38). That call to stay awake leads into chapter 22's account of the night Jesus himself was betrayed.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Praises a poor widow's offering, predicts the temple's destruction, and warns of persecution and cosmic upheaval while urging watchful hope (21:1-36).

keyFigures.name: Poor widow
keyFigures.role: Gives two small coins to the temple treasury, a gift Jesus says is greater than all the wealthy's large contributions (21:1-4).

keyFigures.name: Disciples and hearers
keyFigures.role: Ask Jesus when the temple will be destroyed and what sign will mark it, receiving his long discourse on persecution and the end in response (21:7).

keyFigures.name: False claimants
keyFigures.role: Predicted figures who will come claiming Jesus' own identity and saying the time is near, whom Jesus warns his followers not to follow (21:8).

keyFigures.name: Jerusalem's inhabitants
keyFigures.role: Described by Jesus as facing a coming siege and distress once the city is surrounded by armies (21:20-24).

keyThemes.explanation: A poor widow's two small coins outweigh the large gifts of the wealthy in Jesus' eyes, since she gave everything she had to live on (21:1-4).
Jesus predicts that the temple's impressive stones will be thrown down, a destruction his own first readers had likely already seen happen (21:5-11).
Jesus promises that even persecution and betrayal will become an opportunity for testimony, and that not a hair of their heads will finally perish (21:12-19).
Jesus describes Jerusalem surrounded by armies and the sky itself in upheaval, yet tells his followers to lift up their heads, since their redemption is drawing near (21:20-36).

Luke 22.summary: As Passover approaches, Judas arranges to betray Jesus (Luke 22:1–6). Jesus shares a final meal with the apostles, speaks of bread and cup in relation to his body and covenant, and teaches service rather than rivalry over status (Luke 22:7–38). On the Mount of Olives he prays in distress; Judas arrives with a crowd, Jesus is arrested, and Peter denies knowing him three times (Luke 22:39–62). Jesus is mocked and questioned before the council, where his claims about the Son of Man and Son of God become central (Luke 22:63–71).
Luke 22.whereWeAre: Chapter 21 ended with Jesus teaching daily in the temple while crowds came early each morning to hear him there (21:37-38). Chapter 22 follows him into that final night: as Passover approaches Judas arranges to betray him, Jesus shares a last meal reinterpreting its bread and cup around his own body and covenant, prays in anguish on the Mount of Olives, is arrested, and is mocked and questioned before the council after Peter denies him three times (22:1-71). That council hearing sets up chapter 23's formal trial before Rome's own representatives.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Shares a final Passover meal reinterpreting its bread and cup around his own body and covenant, prays in anguish on the Mount of Olives, and is arrested and questioned before the council (22:1-71).

keyFigures.name: Judas Iscariot
keyFigures.role: A member of the Twelve who arranges to betray Jesus for money and identifies him with a kiss when the armed crowd arrives (22:3-6,47-48).

keyFigures.name: Peter
keyFigures.role: Is warned that Satan desires to sift him, insists he is ready to die with Jesus, and then denies knowing him three times before the rooster crows (22:31-34,54-62).

keyFigures.name: The apostles
keyFigures.role: Share the Passover meal, argue about who is greatest even as Jesus speaks of his coming death, and fall asleep at Gethsemane instead of praying with him (22:14,24,45).

keyFigures.name: High priest's servant
keyFigures.role: Has his ear cut off by one of the apostles during Jesus' arrest, and Jesus heals him on the spot (22:50-51).

keyFigures.name: Chief priests and elders
keyFigures.role: Arrive with the armed crowd to arrest Jesus and later question him before the council, where he is condemned for his own testimony (22:52,66-71).

keyThemes.explanation: At the Passover table Jesus calls the bread his body and the cup the new covenant in his blood, giving his disciples a meal to remember him by (22:14-20).
When the disciples dispute who is greatest, Jesus says the one who leads must be like the one who serves, pointing to his own example at the table (22:24-30).
In Gethsemane Jesus prays so intensely that his sweat falls like drops of blood, submitting to God's will even while wishing the coming suffering could pass (22:39-46).
Peter denies Jesus three times just as predicted, and the Lord's own silent look after the rooster crows is enough to send him out weeping bitterly (22:54-62).

explainedReferences.explanation: Jesus quotes Isaiah about being counted among transgressors.
Same event: Jesus praying on the Mount of Olives before his arrest.
Same event: Judas' arrival with a crowd and Jesus' arrest.
Same event: Peter denying Jesus three times during Jesus' arrest and hearing.
Same event: Peter denying Jesus three times and later weeping.

Luke 23.summary: Jesus is brought before Pilate, who questions him and then sends him to Herod Antipas. Both officials become part of the proceedings, while the crowd demands Barabbas's release and Jesus' crucifixion (Luke 23:1–25). On the way to execution Jesus addresses mourning women, and at the place of crucifixion he is mocked, while one condemned criminal appeals to him (Luke 23:26–43). Darkness and the tearing of the temple veil accompany his death; a centurion responds, and acquaintances and women watch (Luke 23:44–49). Joseph of Arimathea places Jesus' body in a tomb before the Sabbath, observed by women who prepare spices (Luke 23:50–56).
Luke 23.whereWeAre: Chapter 22 ended with the council asking Jesus directly whether he was the Son of God and deciding they needed no further testimony against him (22:70-71). Chapter 23 carries that charge to Pilate and Herod Antipas, both of whom examine Jesus without finding real fault in him, yet Pilate yields to the crowd's demand to release Barabbas and crucify Jesus instead; Jesus is mocked, dies between two criminals, and is buried by Joseph of Arimathea before the Sabbath begins (23:1-56). That burial sets up chapter 24's discovery, after the Sabbath ends, that the tomb is empty.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Is questioned by Pilate and Herod Antipas without either finding real fault in him, is crucified between two criminals, and dies as the temple curtain tears in two (23:1-49).

keyFigures.name: Pilate
keyFigures.role: Finds no fault in Jesus three times, sends him to Herod Antipas, and finally yields to the crowd's demand, releasing the rebel Barabbas and ordering Jesus crucified (23:4,7,13-25).

keyFigures.name: Herod Antipas
keyFigures.role: Hopes to see Jesus perform a miracle, mocks him with his soldiers when Jesus stays silent, and sends him back to Pilate, becoming Pilate's friend that same day (23:7-12).

keyFigures.name: Simon of Cyrene
keyFigures.role: Is made to carry the cross behind Jesus on the way to the execution (23:26).

keyFigures.name: Two condemned criminals
keyFigures.role: Crucified on either side of Jesus; one mocks him while the other asks to be remembered and is promised paradise (23:32-33,39-43).

keyFigures.name: Joseph of Arimathea and the women from Galilee
keyFigures.role: Joseph, a council member who had not agreed with the decision against Jesus, asks for his body and lays it in a new tomb, while the women who had followed Jesus watch and then prepare spices (23:50-56).

keyThemes.explanation: Pilate finds no fault in Jesus three times over but still yields to the crowd's demand, releasing a convicted rebel and murderer in his place (23:1-25).
On the way to his own execution Jesus tells weeping women to weep for themselves instead, and from the cross he promises paradise to a criminal who simply asks to be remembered (23:26-43).
Darkness covers the land and the temple curtain tears as Jesus dies, and even a Roman centurion is moved to call him a righteous man (23:44-49).
Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not agreed with the decision against Jesus, provides a new tomb, while the women who watched prepare spices before resting on the Sabbath (23:50-56).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Jesus being led to crucifixion and crucified.
Jesus repeats the words calling on mountains and hills to cover the people.
Jesus speaks the psalm's words commending his spirit into God's hands.
Same event: Joseph of Arimathea placing Jesus' body in a tomb.

Luke 24.summary: Women who visit Jesus' tomb at dawn find the stone rolled away and the body absent; two men in dazzling garments announce that he has risen. The apostles initially dismiss their report, while Peter inspects the tomb (Luke 24:1–12). Jesus accompanies two disciples on the road to Emmaus, interprets Scripture about the Messiah's suffering, and is recognized in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:13–35). He appears to gathered followers, shows his hands and feet, eats fish, and explains the Scriptures concerning suffering, resurrection, repentance and forgiveness (Luke 24:36–49). Luke ends with Jesus' departure, the disciples' worship, and their return to Jerusalem in joy (Luke 24:50–53).
Luke 24.whereWeAre: Chapter 23 ended with women from Galilee watching where Joseph laid Jesus' body, then resting on the Sabbath as the law commanded (23:55-56). Luke's closing chapter answers that rest: the same women find the tomb empty, two disciples recognize the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus in the breaking of bread, and he appears to the gathered disciples and is carried up to heaven after commissioning them to preach forgiveness to all nations (24:1-53). That commission is where John's Gospel takes up Jesus' story again, from its own distinct beginning in the eternal Word.

keyFigures.name: Jesus
keyFigures.role: Is found risen from the tomb, walks unrecognized with two disciples to Emmaus, and appears to the gathered disciples before being carried up to heaven (24:1-53).

keyFigures.name: Women at the tomb
keyFigures.role: Include Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and others who find the tomb empty and are the first to hear that Jesus has risen (24:1-10).

keyFigures.name: Peter
keyFigures.role: Runs to the tomb after hearing the women's report and goes home wondering at what he sees (24:12).

keyFigures.name: Cleopas and his companion
keyFigures.role: Two disciples walking to Emmaus who are joined by the risen Jesus without recognizing him until he breaks bread at their table (24:13-31).

keyFigures.name: The Eleven and companions
keyFigures.role: Dismiss the women's report as idle tales, then receive the risen Jesus' appearance and his opening of their understanding of Scripture (24:11,36-45).

keyFigures.name: Two radiant men
keyFigures.role: Appear at the empty tomb to announce to the women that Jesus has risen just as he said he would (24:4-7).

keyThemes.explanation: The women's report of an empty tomb and a risen Jesus strikes the apostles as idle talk, though Peter still runs to check for himself (24:1-12).
Two disciples walk seven miles with the risen Jesus without recognizing him until he breaks bread at their table, the same moment that opens their eyes to who he is (24:13-35).

Jesus shows the gathered disciples his hands and feet, eats before them to prove he is not a ghost, and opens their understanding of how the Scriptures pointed to his suffering and resurrection all along (24:36-49).
Luke's Gospel ends not in grief but in worship, as the disciples return to Jerusalem with great joy to wait for the power Jesus promised (24:50-53).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The discovery of the empty tomb, with different witnesses and details.
Same event: The risen Jesus appearing to assembled disciples.
